content: Okra, also referred to as lady's finger, bhindi, or gumbo, is a flowering plant that is cultivated for its edible green fruits. Its scientific name is Abelmoschus esculentus. The plant can grow up to 5 meters in height. Its leaves are palmate, measuring 10–20 cm in length and width, and typically have 5–7 lobes. The flowers are 4–8 cm in diameter, with five petals that range in color from white to yellow, often featuring a red or purple spot at the base of each petal. The fruit is a capsule that can grow up to 20 cm long and contains numerous seeds. The term okra originates from West Africa and is related to the Igbo word ọ́kụ̀rụ̀. In various Bantu languages, it is called kingombo or similar variants, which influenced its name in Portuguese, Spanish, and French. The Arabic name for okra has shaped its terminology in the Middle East, the Balkans, Turkey, North Africa, and Russia. In South Asia, it is commonly referred to as bhindi. Historically, okra was sometimes incorrectly classified under the synonym Hibiscus esculentus L. The plant is believed to have originated in the Ethiopian Highlands, although its exact distribution pathway remains undocumented. By the 12th and 13th centuries, Egyptians and Moors were using the Arabic term for the plant, suggesting its introduction from the east, possibly via the Red Sea or the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait to the Arabian Peninsula, rather than across the Sahara. One of the earliest written accounts of okra cultivation comes from a Spanish Moor who visited Egypt in 1216, describing its use by locals who consumed the tender young pods with meal. From Arabia, the plant spread around the Mediterranean and eastward. The absence of a word for okra in ancient Indian languages suggests its arrival in India after the start of the Common Era. Okra was introduced to the Americas via the Atlantic slave trade by 1658, with its presence recorded in Brazil. It was further documented in Suriname in 1686. By the early 18th century, okra had reached southeastern North America and gradually spread. It was being cultivated as far north as Philadelphia by 1748, and Thomas Jefferson noted its establishment in Virginia by 1781. By 1800, okra was widespread in the southern United States, with the first mention of different cultivars appearing in 1806. Abelmoschus esculentus is cultivated globally in tropical and warm temperate regions for its fibrous fruits or pods, which contain round, white seeds. The immature fruits are harvested and consumed as a vegetable. In countries such as Iran, Egypt, Lebanon, Israel, Jordan, Iraq, Greece, and Turkey, okra is commonly used in thick stews made with vegetables and meat. In Indian cuisine, it is sautéed or added to gravy-based dishes and is particularly popular in South India. By the late 20th century, okra gained popularity in Japanese cuisine, where it is served with soy sauce and katsuobushi or prepared as tempura. In Charleston, okra is used as a thickening agent in gumbo. In the southern United States, breaded and deep-fried okra is a common dish, and the immature pods are sometimes pickled. Okra leaves can be cooked similarly to beet greens or dandelions and are also consumed raw in salads. The seeds can be roasted and ground to create a caffeine-free coffee substitute. During the American Civil War, when imports were disrupted, okra seeds were noted as a viable coffee alternative. Okra is a key ingredient in several regional dishes. In Brazil, frango com quiabo (chicken with okra) is a well-known dish, particularly in the Minas Gerais region. Gumbo, a hearty stew with okra as a primary ingredient, is a staple along the Gulf Coast of the United States. The term gumbo derives from the Central Bantu word for okra, kigombo, which entered Caribbean Spanish as guingambó or quimbombó. Okra is also a traditional component of callaloo, a Caribbean dish and the national dish of Trinidad and Tobago. Okra oil, extracted from the seeds, is a greenish-yellow edible oil with a pleasant taste and odor. It is rich in unsaturated fats, including oleic acid and linoleic acid. The oil content of okra seeds is approximately 40%, and oil yields from okra crops are high, reaching 794 kg/ha in one trial, surpassed only by sunflower oil. Abelmoschus esculentus is one of the most heatand drought-tolerant vegetable species globally. It can thrive in poor soils with heavy clay and intermittent moisture but is susceptible to severe frost, which can damage the pods. In the southern United States, it is grown as an annual crop. Cultivation involves soaking the seeds overnight before planting them at a depth of 1–2 cm. Germination occurs within six days for soaked seeds or up to three weeks otherwise. Seedlings require ample water. The seed pods must be harvested within a week of pollination to remain edible, as they quickly become fibrous and woody. The plant's mucilaginous properties result in a characteristic goo when the seed pods are cooked. To minimize this effect, okra pods are often stir-fried to evaporate moisture or paired with slightly acidic ingredients like citrus or tomatoes. Cooked okra leaves are also effective as a soup thickener.
